I've attached NO2 (Q3 2021 average) data for 33 London boroughs and a list showing which boroughs are geographic neighbors of each other.

Question: You can use a statistical method such as Getis-Ord Gi*, or any other method you choose, to identify boroughs where there is an unusually intense CONCENTRATION of high NO2 (Q3 2021 average) (a HOT spot) or low NO2 (Q3 2021 average) (a COLD spot), considering each borough TOGETHER WITH its neighbors as one combined local area.

This is different from asking whether a borough simply resembles its immediate neighbors -- instead, you are testing whether the COMBINED total (the borough together with its neighbors) is unusually large or small compared to the citywide average, regardless of how similar the borough is to any one neighbor individually.

Note: a borough whose own value is missing should not itself be reported as a hot or cold spot in your final answer. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. Implement your chosen method directly using only pandas and numpy. If your method produces a z-score, use the standard critical values: |z| > 1.96 for 95% confidence, |z| > 2.576 for 99% confidence.

End your response with exactly one line listing every borough you identified, using HOT for hot spot and COLD for cold spot, and including the computed real number (e.g. a z-score) for each:

If you find none, write: FINAL ANSWER: none

import pandas as pd

adjacency_data = pd.read_csv(ADJACENCY_PATH)

Thought: I will create a combined NO2 value for each borough by summing its own NO2 value with those of its neighbors. I will also calculate the mean and standard deviation of the combined values to identify hot and cold spots using z-scores. 

Action:
```python
# Merge the NO2 data with the adjacency data to create a combined dataset
combined_data = adjacency_data.merge(no2_data, on='borough', how='left')

# Create a function to calculate the combined NO2 value for each borough
def calculate_combined_no2(borough):
    neighbors = combined_data[combined_data['borough'] == borough]['neighbor'].values
    combined_values = no2_data[no2_data['borough'].isin([borough] + list(neighbors))]['avg_no2_value']
    return combined_values.sum()

# Calculate combined NO2 values for each borough
no2_data['combined_no2'] = no2_data['borough'].apply(calculate_combined_no2)

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the combined NO2 values
mean_combined_no2 = no2_data['combined_no2'].mean()
std_combined_no2 = no2_data['combined_no2'].std()

# Calculate z-scores for each borough
no2_data['z_score'] = (no2_data['combined_no2'] - mean_combined_no2) / std_combined_no2

# Filter for hot and cold spots
hot_spots = no2_data[(no2_data['z_score'] > 1.96) & (no2_data['avg_no2_value'].notna())]
cold_spots = no2_data[(no2_data['z_score'] < -1.96) & (no2_data['avg_no2_value'].notna())]

hot_spots_result = hot_spots[['borough', 'z_score']]
cold_spots_result = cold_spots[['borough', 'z_score']]

hot_spots_result, cold_spots_result
```

Observation: I have calculated the combined NO2 values and their corresponding z-scores for each borough. Now I will extract the boroughs identified as hot and cold spots along with their z-scores.
